newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Dec 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Dec 23.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Monday:
- Since the Telecommunications Act of 1996 became law, the cable television industry has largely abandoned its foray into the telephone business.
- Interactive television may still be searching for an audience in the home, but there are signs now that it may finally have found a solid market in the business traveler.
- As the holiday shopping season enters its final week, some retailers of consumer electronics and home computers say sales have finally picked up somewhat.
- Two inventors have patented a system that, they say, will allow motorists to dump sand beneath spinning tires merely by pressing a button on the dashboard.
- Postings on the World Wide Web are offering Tickle Me Elmo dolls - which sell for $25 to $30 in stores - for $500 or more.
- While publications aimed at lesbians remain a tough sell, people in the industry say there is a strong potential market.
- On the final weekend before Christmas, shoppers did not appear to be holding on to their wallets as tightly as in previous years.
- Joseph Nacchio, head of AT&T's 's troubled consumer long distance unit, resigned to take over Quest Communications, a company that specializes in leasing fiber-optic lines.

- A Darwinian process that favors proven, broad-concept programming approaches over niche concepts is preventing dozens of small cable television channels from reaching most of the nation's households.

- An advertising industry group has decided not to broaden the focus of self-regulation by reviewing campaigns for so-called age-restricted products like cigarettes, alcoholic beverages and lottery tickets.

- To be sucessful in marrying its software to the Nextstep operating system, Apple Computer will need to quickly woo thousands of Macintosh developers by convincing them that the new Next-Macintosh hybrid will be a strong technical competitor to Microsoft's Windows 95 and NT programs.
